Structural and Modal Analysis of a Wheel Rim
2
1
Introduction
Wheel rims are safety-critical rotating components subject to a wide range of static and cyclic
loads during vehicle operation, as well as dynamic excitation from road roughness, tire non-
uniformity, and rotational imbalance. A thorough structural characterisation of a wheel there-
fore requires both a static structural assessment of stress and deformation under representative
loading, and a modal (free-vibration) assessment of its natural frequencies and mode shapes.
This project presents both types of analysis for a commercially styled multi-spoke wheel rim,
performed in Ansys Mechanical. The rim geometry was designed and modelled in SolidWorks
and subsequently imported into Ansys via SpaceClaim. The report is structured in two parts:
 Part I – Static Structural Analysis: the rim is analysed under (a) a simplified static
radial load representing vehicle weight transmitted through the tire contact patch, and
(b) a bending moment derived from the SAE J328 cornering fatigue test standard, which
is the industry-standard load case used to qualify wheel designs.
 Part II – Modal Analysis: the rim’s natural frequencies and mode shapes are studied
under free-free, bolt-hole-constrained, and a simplified tire-loaded (distributed mass +
radial spring) configuration, preceded by a mesh convergence study.
1.1
Geometry, Material, and Mesh
The wheel rim CAD model was imported into Ansys SpaceClaim 2026 R1 as a single, clean solid
body, with no gaps or surface defects detected. The rim was assigned an Aluminium Alloy
material (Table 1) consistent with the 356.0-T6 permanent-mold cast aluminium alloy identified
in the source CAD file. The same geometry, material, and a converged mesh (Section 5) were
reused across all static and modal analyses in this report for consistency.

Part I
Static Structural Analysis
2
Methodology
Two static structural load cases were analysed, both using a Fixed Support applied to the
cylindrical faces of the five bolt holes (representing the wheel bolted to a hub), and the same
converged mesh used throughout this report.

Structural and Modal Analysis of a Wheel Rim
3
2.1
Case 1: Simplified Radial Load
A vertical (radial) load of 4000 N was applied at a Remote Point located at the bottom of the
outer flange, representing the ground reaction force transmitted through the tire contact patch
under a typical passenger car corner weight (∼400 kg). The load was applied as a Remote Force
with Deformable behaviour, directed toward the fixed hub.
2.2
Case 2: SAE J328 Cornering Bending Moment
To represent a more realistic and structurally demanding loading condition, a bending moment
was applied following the SAE J328 rotating bending fatigue test standard. In the physical
test, the wheel is bolted to a rotating spindle while a stationary arm applies a constant bending
moment at the rim via a bearing, so that every point on the rim cycles through tension and
compression as the wheel rotates. The static configuration analysed here represents a single
instant of that cycle, with the moment applied at the rim’s outer flange edge (same Remote
Point location as Case 1) and the hub fixed at the bolt holes.
The bending moment magnitude was calculated using the standard SAE J328 formula:
M = W × R × µ × S
(1)
where W = 4000 N is the static wheel load, R = 0.30 m is the assumed tire rolling radius,
µ = 1.1 is the standard simulated cornering friction coefficient, and S = 1.5 is the standard
severity/design factor, giving:
M = 4000 × 0.30 × 1.1 × 1.5 ≈2000 N·m
(2)
This moment was applied as a Remote Moment at the same Remote Point used for Case 1,
resolved into in-plane components tangential to the wheel’s circumference at that location, so
that it produces a genuine bending action about the rim rather than a simple torque about the
wheel axis.

The SAE J328 bending case produces roughly six to nine times higher stress, deformation, and
strain than the simplified radial load case, and reduces the safety factor from 13.4 down to
2.1. This is a substantial and physically meaningful difference, and illustrates precisely why the
automotive industry uses the rotating bending fatigue test, rather than a simple static radial
load, as the primary structural qualification test for wheels: the bending case is the governing
(more severe) load condition, and a safety factor of 13 under radial load alone would give a
misleadingly optimistic impression of the design’s structural margin.
In both cases, the maximum stress is located near the spoke-to-hub transition on the loaded
side of the rim – consistent with this region being the classical location where bending load
transitions from the spokes into the hub, and a commonly reported fatigue crack initiation site
in real wheel structures.
It is worth noting that a safety factor of 2.1 against yield under the SAE J328 static case does
not directly indicate the wheel’s actual fatigue life, since the SAE J328 test is fundamentally a
cyclic (rotating) fatigue test; the static analysis performed here captures only a single instant
of that cycle and should be interpreted as a structural stress check rather than a full fatigue-life
prediction.
3.4
Modelling Assumptions and Limitations (Static Analysis)
 The radial and bending loads are both applied as remote loads at a single point on the
flange (representing the tire contact patch / loading arm location), rather than distributed
over a realistic contact patch area.
 The bending moment magnitude uses standard SAE J328 formula inputs (W = 4000 N,
R = 0.30 m, µ = 1.1, S = 1.5); a specific vehicle’s actual corner weight and tire radius
would refine this value.
 The analysis is static, representing a single instant of the SAE J328 rotating bending
cycle; a full fatigue-life assessment would require a rotating or cyclic loading simulation
and S-N fatigue data for the material.
Part II
Modal Analysis

Structural and Modal Analysis of a Wheel Rim
6
4
Methodology
All modal analyses were performed as linear eigenvalue analyses using the Block Lanczos solver,
extracting the first 12 modes in each case, using the same geometry, material, and mesh de-
scribed in Section 5. Three boundary condition configurations were studied:
 Free-Free: no constraints applied. Used to validate the mass and stiffness properties of
the model via the six expected rigid-body modes.
 Constrained: a Fixed Support applied to the cylindrical faces of the five bolt holes,
representing the wheel bolted to a hub.
 Tire-Loaded (Extension): free-free baseline augmented with a Distributed Mass (10 kg
total, representing the tire) applied to the outer flange face, and four longitudinal springs
(50,000 N/m each, 200,000 N/m combined) connecting four symmetric points on the
flange to fixed ground references, arranged at 90◦intervals around the circumference to
approximate distributed radial tire stiffness.
5
Mesh Convergence Study
To ensure the reported natural frequencies were not dependent on mesh density, a convergence
study was performed on the free-free model by tracking the frequencies of Mode 7 (first 2-
nodal-diameter flange bending mode) and Mode 9 (first 3-nodal-diameter flange bending mode)
across four mesh densities, ranging from the default adaptive mesh down to a manually refined
0.0115 m element size (the practical limit of the Ansys Student license used for this project).

Between the medium (0.012 m) and fine (0.0115 m) meshes, Mode 7 changed by only 0.10 Hz

All modal results in this report are reported using this

structural load cases in Part I.
6
Free-Free Modal Analysis
6.1
Overview
The free-free configuration (no boundary conditions) was used first, both as a baseline for
comparison and as a validation check: a correctly modelled free-free structure must exhibit
exactly six rigid-body modes (three translational, three rotational) at approximately 0 Hz,
before any flexible (deformable) modes appear.

6.2
Discussion of Mode Shapes
Modes 1 through 6 were confirmed to occur at (numerically) zero frequency, verifying the correct-
ness of the model’s mass and inertia properties and the absence of any unintended constraints.
The first flexible modes (7–8) form a closely spaced pair at ≈381 Hz, each showing a two-lobe
(2-nodal-diameter) bending pattern concentrated in the outer flange, with the spokes and hub
remaining comparatively rigid (Figure 5a). The close frequency spacing between the pair is
characteristic of near-axisymmetric structures, where the same physical mode shape can occur
in two orthogonal circumferential orientations.
Modes 9–10 (Figure 5b) follow the same pattern but with a 3-nodal-diameter shape, again as
a closely spaced degenerate pair, at ≈772 Hz – consistent with the classical trend in disc/ring
vibration theory, where increasing the number of nodal diameters increases the modal stiffness
and hence the frequency.
Mode 11 (Figure 6) breaks from this pattern: rather than concentrated flange bending, the
entire disc face – spokes and hub together – moves axially in a roughly axisymmetric “umbrella”
or breathing pattern. This is a physically distinct mode family governed primarily by spoke
bending stiffness, rather than flange bending stiffness, and its appearance between the 3-ND and
4-ND flange modes (rather than after them) illustrates that mode number does not necessarily
correspond to increasing shape complexity – different structural mechanisms can interleave in
frequency depending on the specific geometry.
Mode 12 (1249.79 Hz, not shown separately) returns to the flange-bending family, showing a
clear 4-nodal-diameter pattern similar to Modes 7–10 but with one additional lobe.

7.3
Discussion
Fixing the hub via the bolt holes produces two important effects, clearly visible in Table 8:
New mode families appear.
The axisymmetric ring mode (modes 1–2, ≈390 Hz) and
the spoke-bending mode (modes 5–6, ≈680–700 Hz) did not exist in the free-free case. In
the free-free model, this type of motion is mathematically indistinguishable from rigid-body
translation/rotation and is absorbed into the zero-frequency rigid body modes; once the hub is
fixed, these become genuine, distinguishable flexible modes with real, non-zero frequencies.
Higher-order flange modes are largely insensitive to the hub constraint. The 3-nodal-
diameter mode shifts by less than 0.2 Hz (771.8 →780.5 Hz) – essentially unchanged – while
the 2-nodal-diameter mode shifts substantially (381.4 →∼438 Hz, an increase of roughly 15%).
Mode shape visualisation (Figures 7a–9) shows that the higher-order flange modes have their
maximum deformation concentrated in the outer flange, with very little motion at the hub;
consequently, constraining the hub has little effect on their frequency. The 2-ND mode, by
contrast, involves more participation from the hub/spoke region and is therefore more sensitive
to how that region is supported.

8
Tire-Loaded Extension
8.1
Modelling Approach
As an extension to the free-free study, the effect of a mounted tire was approximated using a
simplified lumped model:
 Tire mass: modelled as a Distributed Mass of 10 kg, scoped to the entire outer flange
face, so that mass loading is spread continuously around the circumference rather than
concentrated at discrete points.
 Tire stiffness: modelled as four longitudinal (radial) springs, each of stiffness 50,000 N/m
(200,000 N/m combined), connecting four points on the flange – spaced at 90◦intervals
around the circumference – to fixed ground references along the corresponding radial
directions.
An initial attempt using four discrete point masses (2.5 kg each) at the same four locations,
rather than a distributed mass, was found to have almost no effect on the flange bending mode
frequencies.
This is because the point masses did not align with the regions of maximum
modal displacement around the full circumference, and so did not meaningfully couple with
the flexible mode shapes.
Switching to a distributed mass produced substantial, physically
meaningful frequency shifts, illustrating that the spatial distribution of an approximated mass
or stiffness element – not just its total magnitude – is critical to obtaining a representative
simplified model.

8.3
Discussion
Two new low-frequency modes (5–6, ≈20.8 Hz) appear once the tire springs are introduced.
Mode-shape animation (Figure 10a) shows the entire rim translating almost rigidly against
the four tire springs, with very little internal flexing – analogous to the classical “wheel hop”
or unsprung-mass bounce mode familiar from vehicle dynamics, and a reassuring qualitative
validation that the simplified spring model captures the expected low-frequency behaviour of a
tire-mounted wheel.
All of the higher flexible modes shift down substantially once the tire’s mass is included (Table 9),
by 21–35%. This is consistent with ω ∝
p
k/m: adding participating mass around the flange,
where these modes already have their largest displacement, reduces their natural frequency
without requiring any change in the underlying structural stiffness. The umbrella mode (mode
11) shows the largest relative shift, suggesting its axisymmetric, largely axial motion couples
particularly strongly with the added radial-mass distribution at the flange.

8.4
Modelling Limitations
The tire-loaded model presented here is a first-order approximation intended to illustrate the
qualitative effect of tire mass and stiffness, and has several known limitations worth noting:
 Tire stiffness is lumped at four discrete circumferential locations (though mass is dis-
tributed continuously); a fully distributed spring-mass ring, or a full 3-D tire model with
contact, would give a more accurate representation.
 The assumed tire mass (10 kg) and combined radial stiffness (200,000 N/m) are represen-
tative estimates for a passenger car tire, not measured values for a specific tire.
 Only the free-free baseline was extended with the tire model; a combined constrained-
plus-tire case (representing the fully mounted, tire-loaded wheel) was not analysed but
would be a natural next step.
9
Overall Conclusions
This project combined a static structural assessment and a modal characterisation of a SolidWorks-
modelled multi-spoke wheel rim in Ansys Mechanical. The key findings are summarised below.
9.1
Static Structural Analysis
1. Under a simplified 4000 N radial load, the wheel is very lightly stressed (max. 20.9 MPa,
safety factor 13.4), indicating that a simple static radial load is not the governing design
case for this component.
2. Under the SAE J328 cornering bending moment (2000 N·m), stress, deformation, and
strain all increase by roughly 6–9× relative to the radial case, and the safety factor drops to
2.1 – confirming that the industry-standard bending fatigue test represents a substantially
more severe and structurally meaningful loading condition than a simple radial load.
3. In both load cases, maximum stress concentrates at the spoke-to-hub transition, consistent
with commonly reported fatigue crack initiation sites in real wheel structures.
9.2
Modal Analysis
1. A mesh convergence study confirmed that a 0.0115 m element size (116,074 nodes) pro-
duces mesh-independent frequencies for the modes of interest, with less than 0.3 Hz change
between the two finest meshes studied.
2. The free-free model correctly exhibited six near-zero-frequency rigid body modes, followed
by a clear progression of flange-bending modes (2-ND at 381 Hz, 3-ND at 772 Hz, 4-ND at
1250 Hz) and a distinct axisymmetric umbrella mode at 1171 Hz, validating the model’s
mass and stiffness distribution.
3. Constraining the bolt holes eliminates the rigid-body modes and introduces two new mode
families (an axisymmetric ring mode and a spoke-bending mode) not distinguishable in
the free-free case, while higher-order flange bending modes remain largely insensitive to
the hub boundary condition.

13
4. A simplified tire model (distributed mass + four radial springs) introduced a new low-
frequency “bounce” mode and reduced all higher flexible mode frequencies by 21–35%,
with the spatial distribution of the approximated mass proving far more influential than
its total value alone.
